title: A General First- and Second-Order Numerical Solver for Non-Markovian Quantum State Diffusion
abstract: The numerical simulation of non-Markovian open quantum systems based on the non-Markovian quantum state diffusion (NMQSD) equation is complicated by functional derivatives with respect to the stochastic process. A general numerical framework that directly treats these functional derivatives without relying on prescribed decompositions of the bath correlation function is still lacking. In this work, we derive an analytical solution of the linear NMQSD equation that reveals three elementary structures of the non-Markovian stochastic dynamics: stochastic propagation, functional-derivative insertion, and memory pairing. Based on this structure, we construct a general auxiliary-state framework for arbitrary bath correlation functions. The framework separates the numerical construction into time discretization, memory quadrature, and hierarchy truncation. We then construct first- and second-order schemes and provide diagrammatic transition rules for their explicit implementation. Numerical results verify the expected temporal accuracy and demonstrate the applicability of the proposed methods to different bath correlation functions and multi-level quantum systems.
summary: This paper introduces a general auxiliary-state framework to numerically solve the Non-Markovian Quantum State Diffusion (NMQSD) equation. It analytically decomposes the dynamics into three fundamental structures and develops convergent first- and second-order time-stepping schemes. The resulting methods offer robust tools for simulating open quantum systems with arbitrary memory environments.
main_problem: The primary challenge is developing a general numerical framework to solve the Non-Markovian Quantum State Diffusion (NMQSD) equation, which is complicated by functional derivatives with respect to the stochastic process.
main_result: The authors construct and analyze first- and second-order auxiliary-state schemes that provide rigorous error bounds ($\mathcal{O}(	au)$ or $\mathcal{O}(	au^2)$) for approximating the non-Markovian dynamics.
method: They derive an analytical solution structure revealing three elementary dynamic components (propagation, insertion, pairing) and implement this using a time-discretization auxiliary-state approach.
model_or_system: The system involves open quantum systems whose reduced density matrix evolution is modeled by the linear NMQSD equation. This formalism describes dynamics influenced by an environment with arbitrary bath correlation functions $\alpha(t, s)$.
key_observables: Error bounds for the physical state approximation ($\|\psi_{\emptyset}^n - \phi_{\emptyset}^n\|$), and expectation values like $\langle\sigma_xangle_t$, $\langle\sigma_yangle_t$, $\langle\sigma_zangle_t$.
important_parameters: Time step ($	au$) and total time ($T$); the structure depends on the bath correlation function $\alpha(t, s)$.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on pathwise boundedness of coefficients and uniform integrability of the memory kernel; the first-order scheme explicitly drops contributions from repeated time labels.
figures_summary: Tables summarize the correspondence between NMQSD forms and diagrammatic notations for Propagation, Pairing, and Insertion. Diagrams illustrate the three elementary transitions in the first-order scheme.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by deriving an analytical solution structure, decomposing it into three parts, constructing auxiliary-state schemes (first and second order), and finally providing rigorous error analysis proving convergence rates ($\mathcal{O}(	au)$ and $\mathcal{O}(	au^2)$) for these numerical methods.
why_interesting: This work provides a highly general and mathematically rigorous computational tool for simulating complex open quantum systems where memory effects are crucial, overcoming limitations of previous specialized solvers.

Figure 1 compares the time evolution of ⟨σx⟩, ⟨σy⟩, and ⟨σz⟩for the first- and second-order schemes against the analytical solution. At this time step, the first-order scheme shows visible numerical deviations from the analytical solution, especially in ⟨σz⟩and ⟨σy⟩. In contrast, the second-order scheme agrees well with the reference dynamics for all three observables, showing improved accuracy at the same time step.
